To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
The market encourages too many discoveries.
the market for research portfolios exhibits the following biases.

(1) the market for research projects is not competitive, (2) the market encourages too much investment in research, (3) the market encourages a greater spread in the distribution in the quality of discoveries than would occur in a competitive market, and (4) the market encourages the excessive occurrence of multiple discovery.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the economics of research portfolios.
the economics of research.
the economic analysis of the research process and its consequences for the distribution and use of knowledge.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the market encourages too much research, too much variation in the quality of research, and too much duplication of research.

the market is biased toward the development of too much research, too many discoveries, and too many multiple discoveries, and that it is biased in favor of the discovery of the highest quality projects.
the market encourages the development and dissemination of too many discoveries and of too many low quality ones.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that the standard model of research and development (R&D) is incomplete.
we are not as good at picking winners as we think we are.
we are not only interested in understanding the economic and social impact of research but also in understanding what makes research successful.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the market for research portfolios is biased in the direction of too much risk.
the current research portfolio is too large, with too little diversity.
the market for research is not efficient, and the market for research should not be expected to be efficient.
